1101.t: Unknown. Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *sń̥h₂u or *sn̥h₂eu, which could be derived from a more primary particle *sń̥ (“separated, without”) or the locative of some (hard-to-identify) noun.

1184.t: From Proto-Hellenic *leukós, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“white; light; bright”).

1121.t: An Iranian borrowing, ultimately from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah. Compare native περίβολος (períbolos).

1199.t: From Phoenician 𐤑𐤓 (ṣr), cognate with Biblical Hebrew צוֹר (ṣôr) and Aramaic טור.

1139.t: From Proto-Indo-European *krét-os, from *kret- (“strength; intelligence”). Cognates include Sanskrit क्रतु (krátu), Avestan 𐬑𐬭𐬀𐬙𐬎- (xratu-), and Old English heard (“hard”) (whence English hard).

1178.t: Uncertain. Probably from Proto-Indo-European *wreh₁ǵ- (“to break”); compare Old Armenian երգիծանեմ (ergicanem, “to tear, dissect”), Lithuanian rėžti, and Old Church Slavonic рѣзати (rězati, “to cut, slaughter”).

1186.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kseros (“dry”). Cognates include Latin serescō, Old High German serawēn, Old Armenian չոր (čʻor), Middle Armenian չիր (čʻir), and perhaps Sanskrit क्षार (kṣārá, “sharp, acrid, pungent”).

1180.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₂weks- (“to enlarge”). Cognate with Proto-Germanic *wahsijaną.

1171.t: The etymology surrounding all senses remains somewhat unclear. The fact that the dye came exclusively from Phoenicia assures some connection.

1191.t: Likely from a Proto-Indo-European *gʰelh₂d- (“hail; hoarfrost”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *žȇldъ (“glazed frost, sleet”), Persian ژاله (žâle, “hail”).

1107.t: Substantivized verbal adjective of ἕρπω (hérpō). Compare Latin serpēns and Sanskrit सर्प (sarpá, “snake, serpent”).

1197.t: From Proto-Hellenic *ókʷʰis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ógʷʰis (“snake”). Cognates include Sanskrit अहि॑ (áhi), Avestan 𐬀𐬲𐬌 (aži), Old Armenian իժ (iž), and English ask (“eft; newt; lizard”).

1170.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kʷos (“which”) + -θεν (-then, ablative adverb suffix). Compare its indefinite form ποθέν (pothén).

1136.t: Perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to resemble”), and cognate with ἔοικα (éoika, “to seem (likely that)”), εἴκελος (eíkelos, “like, similar”), εἰκάζω (eikázō, “to portray, liken”), and others; however, no certain cognates exist outside of Greek.

1156.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH- Proto-Indo-European *gʷélHos Ancient Greek βέλος From Proto-Indo-European *gʷélHos, from *gʷelH- (“to throw, pierce”).

1182.t: Uncertain; probably Pre-Greek. Possibly related to Latin digitus, though the details are unclear.

1146.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pórnē, from the Proto-Indo-European root *perh₂- (“to sell”), which also gave the verb πέρνημι (pérnēmĭ, “to sell”).

1167.t: According to Beekes, ultimately of Pre-Greek origin.

1102.t: According to some scholars, from ἄγω (ágō, “to lead, draw out or down”) + -τιος (-tios) (perhaps via an unattested intermediate ἄξις (áxis, “weight”)), with sense development "draw down (in the scale)" > "weigh, import".

1130.t: From ὄψ (óps, “eye”) + -σις (-sĭs). Diachronically from Proto-Hellenic *ókʷtis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ékʷtis, from *h₃ekʷ- (“eye, to see”).

1126.t: Of uncertain origin, though likely from some derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach, attain”) and cognate with Celtic terms like Old Irish éicen (“force, necessity”) (see there for more cognates), as well as perhaps Proto-Germanic *anhtō…

1141.t: From λειτουργός (leitourgós, “public servant”) + -ία (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun–forming suffix).

1144.t: Unknown. It is traditionally compared with ἄχθος (ákhthos), βρόχθος (brókhthos) and ὄχθος (ókhthos).

1124.t: By surface analysis, φέρω (phérō, “to bring, carry”) + -ος (-os). Given the comparison with Sanskrit भर॑ (bhára), the term may be derived from Proto-Hellenic *pʰóros, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰóros (“load, burden”).

1137.t: From Proto-Indo-European *Hyewdʰ-dh-ú-s, from the root *Hyewdʰ- (“become straight”, in most other formations > "targeted motion, assault").

1190.t: Formed from the base of χράομαι (khrắomai, “want, need”) + -μα (-mă).

1164.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-los Proto-Indo-European *yéh₂los Ancient Greek ζῆλος From Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂- (“to go, travel, search, inquire”). Related to Ζητήρ (Zētḗr).

1111.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʷerh₃- Proto-Indo-European *-sḱéti Proto-Indo-European *gʷi-gʷr̥h₃-sḱé-ti Proto-Hellenic *gʷigʷrṓskō Ancient Greek βιβρώσκω From Proto-Hellenic *gʷigʷrṓskō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷi-gʷr̥h₃-sḱé-ti, from…

1168.t: From Proto-Indo-European *wóyde (“to have seen; to know”), from *weyd- (“to see; to know”). Compare εἶδον (eîdon, “to see”) and εἴδομαι (eídomai, “to seem”), which originate from different aspectual forms of the same verbal root.

1143.t: Of uncertain origin. Traditionally derived from a Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“to linger, hesitate, be late”), and connected with Latin prōmellō (“to postpone a court case”), Old Irish mall (“slow, tardy”).

1169.t: From the o-grade of the root of πλέω (pléō, “to sail”) + -ιον (-ion), or inherited directly from Proto-Indo-European *plówyom (“floating vessel”): compare Proto-Germanic *flawją (“ship, vessel”).

1115.t: From δίκαιος (díkaios, “decent, righteous”) + -όω (-óō, “cause someone to be”, factitive verb suffix).

1192.t: From phrases such as ἄλλος ἄλλον (ắllos ắllon), ἄλλοι ἄλλους (ắlloi ắllous, “one another”), with loss of λ either by dissimilation or by the lengthening of α, as well as restoration of the second initial vowel ή (ḗ) (< *h₂élyos (“other”)).

1128.t: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”), the same root of Latin alō, alumnus, oleō and English old.

1185.t: From an older form *λεῖϝος (*leîwos), itself from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁y-u- (“smooth”) and cognate to Latin lēvis (“smooth”).

1163.t: Compound of εὐνή (eunḗ, “bed”) + -οῦχος (-oûkhos, “-holder”); literally, someone who takes care of the nuptial chamber, a chamberlain.

1181.t: From a Semitic source cognate to Hebrew בּוּץ (būṣ, “byssus”) and Aramaic בּוּצָא (būṣā, “byssus”), from Proto-Semitic *būṣ- (“fibrous grass; rush”). Compare also Old Armenian բեհեզ (behez, “byssus”).

1135.t: According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek, due to the presence of an intervocalic -σ- (-s-).

1148.t: From συν- (sun-, “with”) + λέγω (légō, “to choose, to say”).

1120.t: The word may well be Pre-Greek, in view of the suffix "-ακ-".

1166.t: A technical loan of unknown origin. The comparison with καμάρα (kamára, “vaulted chamber”) has little value, while the one with Proto-Slavic *kamy (“stone”) is possible.

1131.t: From ὑπερήφανος (huperḗphanos, “overweening, arrogant; showing oneself above others”) + -ία (-íă, forms feminine abstract nouns) from ὑπέρ (hŭpér, “over, above”) and φανός (phānós, “appearing, shining, bright, resplendent”) from φαίνω (phaínō, “to appear,…

1109.t: Traditionally derived from ὑπερφανής (huperphanḗs, “appearing over; showing oneself above others”), or directly from ὑπέρ (hŭpér, “over, above”) + φανός (phānós, “appearing, shining, bright, resplendent”), in both cases, with epenthetic vowel -η- (-ē-)…

1172.t: From ἀλλαγή (allagḗ, “change”) + -σσω (-ssō), though Beekes considers ἀλλάσσω (ăllắssō) to be original and ἀλλαγή (allagḗ) a derivative. Either way, ultimately from ἄλλος (állos, “other”).

1103.t: From Biblical Hebrew אָסָא (ʾĀsāʾ), from Aramaic אָסְיָא (ʾāsyā, “physician, doctor, healer”), from Akkadian 𒀀𒍪 (A.ZU /⁠asû⁠/) from Sumerian 𒀀𒍪 (A.ZU /⁠azu⁠/, “physician, healer”); compare Classical Syriac ܐܵܣܝܵܐ (ʾāsyā, “healer, physician, medical…

1149.t: From ἀπο- (apo-, back again) + καθίστημι (kathístēmi, to set, place, constitute, appoint).

1162.t: From Proto-Indo-European *demh₂- (“to domesticate, tame”) with the same *-l- suffix as found in δαμάλης (damálēs).
